planting.note: Plant dormant canes or containerized transplants in late winter through early spring, spacing to allow good airflow in Gulf Coast humidity.

directions: Sweet-Ark Picasso is a thornless erect blackberry from the University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture fruit breeding program's Sweet-Ark series, bred for high sugar content and firm texture suited to fresh-market and home-garden use. Self-supporting canes need only minimal trellising. Grow in full sun with consistent moisture and remove spent floricanes after harvest to make room for new primocanes.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture fruit breeding program
University of Arkansas Cooperative Extension Service

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring and train the semi-erect canes to a simple wire trellis.

directions: Dirksen Thornless arose as a natural thornless bud mutation discovered by an Illinois grower in a planting of the thorny heirloom cultivar Eldorado in the mid-1960s, becoming one of the first commercially available thornless erect blackberries. It carries much of Eldorado's cold hardiness and vigor, producing medium-sized, well-flavored black fruit on semi-erect canes. It was historically important as an early parent in thornless blackberry breeding, though it has since been largely surpassed in fruit quality by newer University of Arkansas releases.
sources: USDA ARS historical cultivar records
University of Illinois Extension
Missouri State University Extension fruit variety records

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring; vigorous erect canes benefit from a support wire to keep heavy crops off the ground.

directions: Smoothstem is an erect thornless blackberry released from the USDA's Beltsville, Maryland fruit breeding program in the 1970s, among the first generation of thornless erect cultivars developed alongside Thornfree and Dirksen Thornless. It is vigorous and reliably productive, though its fruit is generally considered softer and less flavorful than later University of Arkansas releases such as Navaho and Ouachita. It remains of mainly historical interest today, valued more for its role in early thornless-blackberry breeding than for fresh-market quality.
sources: USDA Agricultural Research Service historical release records
North Carolina State Extension
University of Maryland Extension

planting.note: Plant dormant trailing canes in late winter to early spring and train onto a trellis; performs best where summers are mild and humidity moderate.

directions: Cascade is a historic Pacific Northwest trailing blackberry released around 1949 from Oregon breeding work, prized for its intensely aromatic, richly flavored fruit reminiscent of wild blackberries. Its long trailing canes require trellising and the variety is susceptible to cane diseases and generally lower-yielding than modern trailing types, which led to it being largely replaced commercially by cultivars like Marion and Olallie. It is still sought out by home gardeners and small specialty growers in cooler climates mainly for its exceptional flavor.
sources: Oregon State University Extension
USDA Agricultural Research Service Corvallis historical variety records

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring in cool-summer gardens; support with a wire trellis.

directions: Malling Centenary is a summer-fruiting floricane red raspberry bred at East Malling Research in Kent, England, and named to mark the research station's hundredth anniversary. It is valued commercially and in gardens across the UK for vigorous, well-anchored canes, consistently heavy yields, and firm, bright-red berries with excellent dessert flavor. Like most red raspberries it performs best where summers are cool, so in the Gulf South it is primarily a cool-season novelty rather than a reliable producer.
sources: East Malling Research / NIAB EMR variety records
Royal Horticultural Society plant records

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring; vigorous upright canes benefit from trellis support in exposed sites.

directions: Malling Admiral is a mid-season floricane red raspberry released by England's East Malling Research in the 1970s and long popular in British home gardens. It produces vigorous, upright canes with good resistance to root rot and reliably heavy crops of firm, well-flavored berries suited to fresh eating and preserving. It remains a benchmark mid-season dessert raspberry in cool-summer climates, though it is not well adapted to Gulf Coast heat and humidity.
sources: East Malling Research historical variety records
Royal Horticultural Society plant records

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil; this cultivar was bred partly for improved root rot tolerance.

directions: Malling Juno is an early-to-midseason floricane red raspberry bred at East Malling Research to extend the start of the raspberry harvest ahead of standard midseason cultivars. It was selected for strong cane vigor and improved tolerance of Phytophthora root rot compared with older raspberry varieties, along with large, firm, good-flavored fruit. Give it well-drained soil and a sheltered site, since like most Malling-series raspberries it is bred for the cool, humid summers of the UK rather than the Gulf South.
sources: East Malling Research / NIAB EMR variety records
James Hutton Institute raspberry breeding history references

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring in cool-summer gardens; a historic late-season home-garden and processing variety.

directions: Taylor is a historic red raspberry released by the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva in 1935, notable for very large, firm, deep-red berries with excellent flavor on a late-ripening floricane. It became an important home-garden and processing variety across the Northeast and upper Midwest for decades, and its fruit quality made it a frequently used parent in later raspberry breeding programs. It requires cool summers and well-drained, fertile soil, and like most heirloom red raspberries struggles with heat and humidity outside its native range.
sources: Cornell University Geneva (NYSAES) historical variety records
USDA National Plant Germplasm System

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring; bred for machine harvest, so canes tolerate firm handling well.

directions: Sumner is a floricane red raspberry developed for Pacific Northwest processing production, selected for firm fruit that holds up well to mechanical harvest, freezing, and canning. Its moderate vigor and reasonably good disease tolerance made it a dependable choice in commercial fields through the latter twentieth century, complementing the more widely planted Willamette and Meeker. It is best suited to the cool, relatively dry summers of its native growing region rather than the hot, humid Gulf Coast.
sources: Washington State University Extension
USDA Agricultural Research Service Corvallis historical variety records

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring in well-drained soil; bred in part for improved root rot tolerance.

directions: Chilliwack is a floricane red raspberry released from the Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada breeding program at the Pacific Agri-Food Research Centre in Agassiz, British Columbia. It ripens in the midseason window with good size, firmness, and flavor, and was developed in part to offer improved root rot tolerance over older Pacific Northwest raspberry cultivars. Give it well-drained soil, consistent moisture, and a cool-summer site for best performance, as it is not well suited to Gulf Coast heat.
sources: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada variety records
British Columbia Ministry of Agriculture publications

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring in well-drained, fertile soil; ripens earlier than most Pacific Northwest raspberries.

directions: Comox is an early-season floricane red raspberry from the British Columbia Agriculture Canada breeding program, notable for ripening well ahead of the standard cultivar Meeker. The large, richly flavored berries are relatively soft, making this variety best suited to fresh eating and home preserving rather than long-distance shipping. It shares the cool-summer preferences of its Pacific Northwest breeding origin and performs poorly in hot, humid climates.
sources: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada variety records
British Columbia Ministry of Agriculture publications

planting.note: Plant dormant canes in early spring; fruits on current-season primocanes, so canes can be mowed to the ground each winter for a single late-summer-to-fall crop.

directions: September is a fall-bearing, primocane-fruiting red raspberry released by the New York State Agricultural Experiment Station in Geneva in 1968. It bears a late-summer-into-fall crop on first-year canes and became historically important as a breeding parent used in developing many of the modern everbearing raspberries that followed, including Heritage. Because it fruits on current-season canes, the whole planting can be mowed down each winter, simplifying pruning compared with traditional summer-bearing types, though it still prefers the cooler summers of its northern origin.
sources: Cornell University Geneva (NYSAES) historical variety records
USDA National Plant Germplasm System
